name: Efavirenz
route_note: oral tablet once daily, usually at bedtime on an empty stomach
originator: Merck & Co.; developed and marketed in the US by DuPont Pharmaceuticals

discovery.note: Benzoxazinone NNRTI licensed to DuPont Merck for development. Year is the priority date of the Merck benzoxazinone patent (US 5,519,021).

tagline: Once-daily NNRTI that anchored first-line HIV therapy worldwide for over a decade
summary: Efavirenz is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor that was a preferred first-line HIV drug worldwide for more than a decade, most famously in the single-tablet Atripla. Its central nervous system side effects (vivid dreams, dizziness, mood changes) and a low genetic barrier to resistance led to its replacement by dolutegravir in most guidelines.
mechanism: Efavirenz binds a hydrophobic pocket near, but not at, the active site of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase. This non-competitive binding distorts the enzyme and blocks DNA polymerisation.
It has no activity against HIV-2 or against reverse transcriptase from other organisms. A single mutation such as K103N gives high-level resistance and cross-resistance to nevirapine.
uses: HIV-1 infection in adults and children in combination with other antiretrovirals

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Sustiva is approved in September 1998, the first antiretroviral approved for once-daily dosing in combination therapy.

history.title: Atripla
history.detail: Efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil becomes the first complete HIV regimen in a single daily pill.

history.title: WHO first line
history.detail: WHO guidelines recommend efavirenz-based fixed-dose combinations as preferred first-line therapy.

history.title: Lower dose
history.detail: WHO endorses efavirenz 400 mg as an alternative based on the ENCORE1 trial.

history.title: Shift to dolutegravir
history.detail: WHO recommends dolutegravir-based regimens as preferred first line, and efavirenz use declines.

pk.half_life: about 52–76 h after a single dose, 40–55 h at steady state
pk.bioavailability: increased by food (taken fasting to reduce side effects)
pk.metabolism: hepatic, mainly CYP2B6 (also CYP3A4); induces its own metabolism and CYP3A

serious: psychiatric symptoms including depression and suicidal ideation
late-onset neurotoxicity including ataxia and encephalopathy
teratogenicity concerns in early pregnancy (largely set aside by later data)

facts: People with slow-metaboliser CYP2B6 variants, more common in some African populations, have higher blood levels and more CNS effects.
Efavirenz can cause false-positive urine cannabinoid tests.
